If your'e lost, the answer of course is to go back to fundamentals, the best explanations of which you're more likely to find in basic and advanced mathematics references, not statistics ones.

As I understand them, the symbol for sigma (Σ) refers to summation, while pi (Π) refers to a product.  Hope that gets you started.

software, or how to run their analysis on clusters or the cloud.

Cheers,
Luiz Irber

Hi Everyone,

I’m trying to automate plotting for all combinations of variables of a reasonably large dataset. I found some code that would suit my purposes online, but it’s not very well annotated (https://stackoverflow.com/questions/10239497/ggplot2scatterplots-for-all-possible-combinations-of-variables), and I'm fairly new to for loops.

I’d like to vary the x and y variables of the scatterplot, but also include a z variable that adjusts the size of the points. The dataframe name is ‘pass’ and I have a series of categorical and continuous variables (listed) though I’m only interested in plotting the continuous variables here. Any assistance would be appreciated.

Best,

Suzanne

############VARIABLE NAMES##############
  # Species identifier fields for relational databases:_kF_IocId _kF_UIocId
#Categorical & their indicator variables#################
  #SppCode, Order, Suborder, Family, ScientificName, JetzName, Region, Regind, NestType, Cupind
  #IncType, IncInd, ParentType, Parind, Mig, MigInd, PlumageDimorph, ForageStrata, BaseGuild

#CAT VAR: AdBehav_Eggs, AdBehav_Kids, AdDep_Eggs, AdDep_Kids, AdMode_Eggs, AdMode_Kids, AdVocal_Eggs, AdVocal_Kids

  #BC_Brain, BC_Carcass, BC_Fat, BC_FlightMus,BC_Gallbladder, BC_Gizzard, BC_Hrt, BC_Int

  MAT <- outer(x, x, paste)

  #  title <- paste(“~/Figures_Matrix", x2, "_", x2, "_", x3, ".png", sep="")
    NAMES <- colnames(df)[cn]

      scale_x_continuous(name=NAMES[1]) +
      scale_y_continuous(name=NAMES[2])
    dev.new <http://dev.new>()
    print(p)
  }

  apply(combs,  1, function(x) plotter(cn=x))

Ah, I see I was overthinking this.  I really don't know where you
would find more than a very-brief description of those topics,
although I suppose there must be books that talk about them in some
detail.  (When I studied this stuff the Greeks didn't yet have an
alphabet.)

But let me add:

(1) I still think the web is a good place to look for discussions of
summations and products.

(2) This is indeed not really a topic for this mailing list (but a
friend in need is a friend indeed).

(3) If you don't already know a programming language, you should
probably learn one, if for no other reason than that you could then
get authoritative answers to questions you might have.  As a trivial
example, in R (the subject of this list) you can compute sums and
products:

> sum(1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8)
[1] 20
> prod(1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8)
[1] 240
>

So, come up with a paper-and-pencil solution, then check it with R (or
Python or ...).

messages.body_plain:
you could also just use plot() on your data-frame, which will precisely draw a plot for every combination of the variables

plot(swiss)

If you use ggplot2, you should use the facetting system instead of for loops. This requires you to reshape your data in a weird form, see code below:

library(tidyverse)

## reshape
swiss_l <- swiss %>%
  rownames_to_column() %>%
  gather(variable, value, -rowname) %>%
  left_join(swiss %>% rownames_to_column(), by = "rowname") %>%
  gather(variable2, value2, -rowname, -variable, -value) %>%
  as_tibble

## plot
swiss_l %>%
  filter(variable!=variable2) %>%  #
  ggplot(aes(x = value, , y= value2)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_grid(variable~variable2)

Matthieu

Hi R-learners,

I’m not sure if this is a coding issue or a mis-understanding of the underlying statistics on my part, but I’m hoping someone can at least point me in the right direction.

I’m modeling density of seedlings after a fire, with data taken over three years, using the lme() function from the nlme package. Replicates are at the plot level, with average seedling density “count.”  I’ve included “plot.code” as a random effect because each plot was sampled three times (“postfire.year”) and I don’t want to pseudo-replicate.

I’m interested in both the effects of soil type (“soil”, a discrete variable which is either “S” for serpentine soils or “N” for non-serpentine soils) and within-type soil characteristics (“pc.1” and “pc.2” which are continuous PCA scores from a variety of other soil data). For simplicity’s sake I’m just going to talk about “pc.1” but the same issues apply to “pc.2”as well.

A sample of the dataframe looks like this:
   plot.code       soil     pc.1      pc.2          count    postfire.year
1 N_LC_17_B    N 1.862677 1.2217352   3.2             1
2 N_LC_17_B    N 2.340146 0.4892991   3.2             1
3 N_LC_17_B    N 1.862677 1.2217352   0.4             2
4 N_LC_17_B    N 2.340146 0.4892991   0.4             2
5 N_LC_17_B    N 1.862677 1.2217352   1.4             3
6 N_LC_17_B    N 2.340146 0.4892991   1.4             3

I care more about the differences between soil types than the PCA scores, and I’m only interested in the within-soil-type effects of the PCA scores.

When I set up my model with a full cross between soil type (“soil”), the differences between soil types get obscured by pc.1 because pc.1 is related to soil type. However, the returned fixed effect structure is as I expect (main soil type term, main pc.1 term, and the interaction term)

summary(lme(count ~ soil*pc.1,
            random= ~1|plot.code,
            data=filter(seed.dens.obligate)))

Fixed effects: count ~ soil + pc.1 * soil
                 Value Std.Error  DF    t-value p-value
(Intercept)  1.9013061 2.0324224 329  0.9354877  0.3502
soilS        2.2164100 2.3048897  65  0.9616122  0.3398
pc.1        -0.1470138 0.9833641 329 -0.1495009  0.8812
soilS:pc.1   0.2734306 1.1453799 329  0.2387248  0.8115

What I’d like to do is run a model with just a main effect for soil, and then the interaction between soil type and pc.1 But when I do this, there are now two interaction terms in the model output, one for each soil type.

summary(lme(count ~ soil + pc.1:soil,
            random= ~1|plot.code,
            data=filter(seed.dens.obligate)))

Fixed effects: count ~ soil + pc.1:soil
                 Value Std.Error  DF    t-value p-value
(Intercept)  1.9013061 2.0324224 329  0.9354877  0.3502
soilS        2.2164100 2.3048897  65  0.9616122  0.3398
soilN:pc.1  -0.1470138 0.9833641 329 -0.1495009  0.8812
soilS:pc.1   0.1264168 0.5872735 329  0.2152605  0.8297

I haven’t had this issue when setting up a similar model formula using lm() when only taking one year of data (without the random effect). Any ideas for 1. Why I’m getting two interaction terms 2. If there’s a better way to do this?

I’ve attached a simplified dataset.

Thanks in advance,
Chhaya

~

> On Oct 3, 2018, at 4:42 PM, Evan Eskew <eve...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi Chhaya,
>
> I don't have time for a more in-depth explanation right now, but basically notice that your parameter estimates are really just getting rearranged. All your estimates are the same between the two models except for the last term. When you force lme() to exclude a main effect of soil, you're simply forcing the algebra to operate differently. In this case, soilS:pc.1 in model 2 equals pc.1 + soilS:pc.1 from model 1. Think of it this way: let's say you want the mean estimate for S soil and and a PC1 score of 2.3 (just made that up).
>
> In model 1: (Intercept)  + soilS  + 2.3 * (pc.1  + soilS:pc.1)
> In other words, you have to factor in the interaction term since you're considering the influence of PC1 in S soil. The interaction term is telling you how the effect of PC1 is modified if you're in S soil. So in order to get the total effect of PC1 in S soil you take the standard PC1 estimate (which applies to N soil) and modify it with the interaction term.
> This equals: 1.9013061 + 2.2164100 + 2.3 * (-0.1470138 + 0.2734306)
>
> In model 2: (Intercept)  + soilS  + 2.3 * (soilS:pc.1)
> You forced the model to drop the default PC1 term, which just resulted in a re-factoring of the math.
> This equals: 1.9013061 + 2.2164100 + 2.3 * (0.1264168)
>
> So it's working out exactly the same.
>
> I'm unclear what your exact goal is, but I'd be cautious about what you seem to be trying to do. Including an interaction without the main effect is likely to lead to a world of confusion. And if you're trying to estimate the effect of being in S soil, the effect of being in N soil, and the effect of PC1 within each of those soil types then you need exactly four parameters. Both of your models contain four parameters, in total have the exact same information, and address that question. You just asked the model to apportion out the algebra differently.

software, or how to run their analysis on clusters or the cloud.

messages.body_plain:
Dear D-RUG,

We're running a little DataFest visualization challenge at the Data Science Initiative and have room for a few more teams. I invite you to participate! Event date for presenting your team's viz is next Thursday, Nov 1 from 2-3pm in the DSI. Teams can be undergrads or grads/postdocs. See details, below, and feel free to contact me or Jane with any questions. All are welcome to attend the final presentation session on Nov 1.

Election day is coming up and this year there are ELEVEN propositions on the ballot.  To make our civic duty more enjoyable and get some data science practice, the Data Science Initiative is hosting an invite-only visualizations focused DataFest to get ready.

To participate, claim a propositions here <https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1egi6KYDX0utRablIY9mN5DfeJdsfeF0fkUiVXCfEGDY/edit?usp=sharing>. Act fast to make sure that you get the proposition that you want! Only one team is allowed per proposition to compete, but we encourage all who are interested to try the challenge on their own.

Create ONE data visualization that helps explain the issue. It can be any type you want, and you're encouraged to try a new type of visualization or software. You can use any type of data from anywhere that is available to you. (See here <http://spatial.ly/r/> and here <https://flowingdata.com/category/visualization/> and here <https://www.r-graph-gallery.com/all-graphs/> for inspiration.) Make sure that your visualization is replicable. Teams can be 1-3 people per proposition.

Presentations are on Thursday, Nov 1st from 2-3pm in the DSI (Shields 360). To compete, present an overview of your selected proposition (including pros and cons) and your visualization in under 5 minutes. (Reading the state vote guide <http://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/pdf/> and a couple newspaper articles is a good place to start for preparing the overview.) Use no more than 2 slides for your presentation, and include a link to your repo with the data, code, etc. on the sign up sheet. Email your presentation slides to plrey...@ucdavis.edu BEFORE 2pm on Nov 1st to compete.

Vote! The best presentation will win a prize. You must be present at the Nov 1 meeting to win. All are welcome to attend the presentations.

Questions? Email plrey...@ucdavis.edu or jaca...@ucdavis.edu.

Hi all,

I have 2 very big data frames that have coordinates x and y, and I want to bring some columns (in this case is just NDVI, in my real data frame I have 13 columns) of the dataframe "b" into the dataframe "a" only if those coordinates x and y match. Here is a reproducible example:

> a
   x y NDVI

6 12 2  0.7
7 10 3  0.5
8 11 3  0.6
9 12 3  0.7

merge(a, b, by.x= c("x", "y"), by.y= c("x", "y"))

   x y NDVI.x NDVI.y

2 11 3    0.6    0.9
3 12 3    0.7   0.95

   x y NDVI NDVI.b
1 10 1  0.5     NA
2 11 1  0.6     NA

5 11 2  0.6     NA

7 10 3  0.5   0.80
8 11 3  0.6   0.90
9 12 3  0.7   0.95

Any ideas on how to do this? Any help is much appreciated!
Best,
Ana

I think you're looking for a left join <https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/reference/join.html>; the best implementation is in tidyverse:

v<-c(rep(1, times=3), rep(2, times=3), rep(3, times=3))
a <- data.frame("x" = rep(c(10:12), times=3), "y"=v, "NDVI" = rep(c("0.5", "0.6", "0.7"), times=3))

w<-c(rep(3, times=3), rep(4, times=3), rep(5, times=3))
b <- data.frame("x" = rep(c(10:12), times=3), "y"=w, "NDVI" = rep(c("0.8", "0.9", "0.95"), times=3))

library(tidyverse)
left_join(a, b, by=c('x', 'y'))
   x y NDVI.x NDVI.y

1 10 1    0.5   <NA>
2 11 1    0.6   <NA>

6 12 2    0.7   <NA>
7 10 3    0.5    0.8

8 11 3    0.6    0.9

Hope this helps,
Vince

Hi all,

we will be having a Meet and Analyze Data session from 3:00pm-5:00pm
today (10/31),
in the 1011 Valley Hall room (http://campusmap.ucdavis.edu/?b=178).
Hope to see you there!

--

If you think you are going to join us, please let us know --

https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSeUW5QS55uDwDpusGYerY542D_tQubkmPMtUKlGdbmoSWfSSQ/viewform

--

Meet and Analyze Data (MAD) is a forum to bring your biological big
data and discuss high level concept problems (what is metagenome
assembly?) and low level coding problems (what does this error message
even mean?!) and everything in between. There is no scheduled or
specific activity: people show up with questions about how to analyze
their data, or maybe they are willing to help others. We typically get
questions about experimental design for
transcriptomic/metagenomic/genomic projects, or how to install
software, or how to run their analysis on clusters or the cloud.

Cheers,
Luiz Irber

messages.body_plain:
Hey all,

I've got some data with blank lines that should interpreted literally instead of converting to <NA>, so I set na.strings to null:

r <- read.csv(filename, stringsAsFactors=FALSE, encoding="UTF8", na.strings=NULL)

This appears to work fine, but it's making a simple sapply function behave strangely:

>read.csv(filename, stringsAsFactors=FALSE, encoding="UTF8", na.strings=NULL)
>
> #check for missing conversions
> u <- unique(v)
> i <- which(! u %in% r$varname)
> u[i]
[1] NA
> length(u[i])
[1] 1

> val <- sapply(u[i], function(x) isTRUE(x == "NA") | is.na <http://is.na>(x))
> val
<NA>
TRUE

If I check the sapply conditions manually, it returns TRUE without the weird <NA>.
> test <- u[i]
> isTRUE(test == "NA") | is.na <http://is.na>(test)
[1] TRUE

This problem goes away if I remove na.strings=NULL from read.csv, but then it breaks a different part of the code where I need a blank to not be converted to NA. In short, something weird is going on that I can't figure out.

Example code/data attached.

Thanks,
Erica

--
Erica Rettig
Ph.D. Candidate
Graduate Group in Ecology, UC Davis
